# fo-intel

Family office intelligence: a pipeline that discovers family offices from public
sources and proves what each one is, and a product that makes the result
queryable in plain English.

**Live system:** https://fo-intel-web.vercel.app

Built for the PolarityIQ Differentiator. **Stage 2 is the current state**; see
[`docs/ACCEPTANCE_M3.md`](docs/ACCEPTANCE_M3.md) for the requirement-to-evidence
matrix and the deliverable index, and [`SUBMISSION.md`](SUBMISSION.md) for the
Stage 1 one, kept as history.

| surface | what it is |
|---|---|
| [`/`](https://fo-intel-web.vercel.app/) | plain-English search over the original Stage 1 corpus of 50 records |
| [`/shortlist`](https://fo-intel-web.vercel.app/shortlist) | the Stage 2 retrieval extension — filters, evidence grading, pagination over all 581 records |
| [`/agent`](https://fo-intel-web.vercel.app/agent) | the agent, using retrieval as a tool |
| [`/operations`](https://fo-intel-web.vercel.app/operations) | what ran, what it refused, and why |

Stage 2 documents: [architecture notes](docs/ARCHITECTURE_NOTES.md) ·
[inclusion standard](docs/INCLUSION_RUBRIC.md) ·
[build summary](docs/BUILD_SESSION_SUMMARY.md) ·
[AI working-session record](docs/ai-session/) ·
[exports](exports/)

---

## What it does

The pipeline finds candidate firms across four independent source classes, proves
what each firm actually is, enriches the ones that qualify, and writes records
where **every value carries its basis** — the exact evidence span it was read
from, the URL and tier of that source, the content hash at the time, and the
outcome of six validation gates under a named policy version. Stage 1 delivered
50 such records; Stage 2 operates the same contract at scale, unattended, on a
schedule. The product reads those records and answers questions about them
without being able to claim anything the records do not support.

The two halves share nothing but the database. The pipeline writes; the app reads.

## Layout

```
packages/core       the record schema, shared by pipeline and app
packages/pipeline   discovery, classification, enrichment, validation, emit
packages/db         Postgres access and hybrid retrieval
packages/rag        query parsing, answer generation, the grounding control
apps/web            the customer-facing product
docs/               methodology, validation chains, RAG notes, Task 2
data/               the delivered dataset, audit trails, run logs
```

## Running it

Requires Node 20+ and a `.env` (copy `.env.example`). Not every key is needed for
every command — the app needs three, the pipeline needs the rest.

```bash
npm install
```

**Inspect the delivered dataset** — no credentials needed beyond the database:

```bash
npx tsx packages/pipeline/src/emit/stats.ts
```

Prints every figure quoted in `SUBMISSION.md`. These are generated rather than
typed, so a stale number in the documentation shows up as a mismatch here.

**Check credentials** before running anything that calls out:

```bash
npx tsx packages/pipeline/src/lib/check-env.ts
```

Makes a real call against each service and reports pass or fail per credential.
It never prints a key.

**Rebuild the dataset** from the candidate pools already in `data/`:

```bash
npx tsx packages/pipeline/src/emit/run.ts
```

**Load it into Postgres and embed it:**

```bash
npx tsx packages/db/src/migrate.ts     # schema, safe to re-run
npx tsx packages/pipeline/src/emit/ingest.ts
```

**Run the product locally:**

```bash
npm run dev -w @fo/web
```

**Evaluate the grounding control:**

```bash
npx tsx packages/pipeline/src/eval/rag-eval.ts
```

15 adversarial cases, two thirds of which the system is supposed to *refuse*.
Reports false negative and false positive rates. Free-tier providers meter tokens
per minute, so `EVAL_PACE_MS=15000` in front of the command avoids measuring the
rate limiter instead of the control.

1138	### Reachability is two metrics, never one
1139	
1140	Because A1 is a judgement a reviewer may not share, reachability is carried through
1141	the entire system as **two independent counts**:
1142	
1143	| Metric | Counts | Projected |
1144	|---|---|---|
1145	| `strict_reachable` | email or phone that demonstrably reaches the named individual. Profiles excluded. | ~60 |
1146	| `profile_assisted_reachable` | the above, **plus** verified personal profiles under A1 | ~160 |
1147	
1148	Both are computed at every checkpoint, stored on the entity, reported in the
1149	dataset, displayed in the product, and stated in the submission. Neither is ever
1150	presented alone or blended into a single headline. See ADR-11.
1151	
1152	If the final counts are short they ship as measured, with this evidence attached.
1153	
1154	Assumptions A1–A5 are recorded in `SPIKE_REACHABILITY.md` and are the audit trail
1155	for this decision.
1156	
1157	### D2 · Minimum qualifying-record standard
1158	
1159	A record counts toward the 500 only when **all** hold:
1160	
1161	| # | Requirement | Gate |
1162	|---|---|---|
1163	| 1 | **Identity resolved** — one real entity, not a duplicate or an unmerged variant | 4 |
1164	| 2 | **Family-office function evidenced** — affirmative evidence of managing family wealth, not merely family ownership (§9) | 2, 7 |
1165	| 3 | **Named human decision-maker** — a person, not a corporate controller | 3 |

1171	independently, because conflating them would let a thin-but-reachable record
1172	qualify and a rich-but-unreachable one fail.
1173	
1174	### D3 · Field-class refresh policies
1175	
1176	Per-field twice-daily refresh is ~6,000 fetches/day at 500 records and would
1177	dominate every other cost. Replaced by four classes with rotating re-observation:
1178	
1179	| Class | Fields | TTL | Cycle behaviour |
1180	|---|---|---|---|
1181	| **Statutory** | registered address, company number, incorporation, control register | 30d | rotate ~1/30th of the set per cycle |
1182	| **Volatile** | principal, title, contact routes, website | 7d | rotate ~1/7th per cycle |
1183	| **Append-only** | dated signals, filings | never | never re-observed; new ones appended |
1184	| **Derived** | classification, commercial completeness | on input change | recomputed when a source claim changes |

########## packages/core/src/schema.ts
/**
 * The record contract. Imported by both the pipeline and the web app so that
 * anything rendered to a user is the same shape the pipeline validated.
 */

export type SourceClass =
  | 'regulatory' // SEC, IRS, other statutory filings
  | 'registry' // company registries, state SOS, Companies House
  | 'primary_web' // the firm's own site or its principals' own profiles
  | 'third_party' // press, conference programmes, job boards
  | 'vendor'; // paid/freemium data services - always named

export interface Evidence {
  sourceUrl: string;
  sourceClass: SourceClass;
  /** How the value was confirmed. Surfaced to the user verbatim, so write it in plain English. */
  method: string;
  observedAt: string;
  /** Named plainly whenever a commercial service touched this value. */
  vendor?: string;
}

export type CellStatus =
  | 'verified' // published on an authoritative source and checked
  | 'inferred' // derived (e.g. email pattern) and not independently confirmed
  | 'could_not_verify' // looked for it, could not establish it
  | 'rejected'; // our own validation found it invalid - must not ship

/**
 * No high-value value is ever a bare primitive. A cell carries its own basis,
 * which is what lets the UI show provenance without the pipeline and the app
 * having to agree on a side channel.
 */
export interface Cell<T> {
  value: T | null;
  status: CellStatus;
  evidence: Evidence[];
  /** 0-1. Drives the retrieval confidence gate, not just display. */
  confidence: number;
  /** Reason, when status is could_not_verify or rejected. */
  note?: string;
}

export type FirmType =
  | 'single_family_office'
  | 'multi_family_office'
  | 'advisory_or_wealth_manager'
  | 'unconfirmed';

/**
 * Firm type is held to a stricter standard than any individual cell: a cell may
 * be honestly uncertain, a firm may not. `qualifies` is false unless we hold
 * affirmative evidence of what the firm actually is.
 */
export interface Classification {
  type: FirmType;
  evidence: Evidence[];
  /** Rule ids from docs/INCLUSION_RUBRIC.md that fired for this firm. */
  rulesMatched: string[];
  confidence: number;
  qualifies: boolean;
  note?: string;
}

export type DiscoveryChannel =
  | 'sec_13f'
  | 'sec_13dg'
  | 'sec_form_d'
  | 'sec_adv'
  | 'irs_990pf'
  | 'companies_house'
  | 'state_registry'
  | 'conference_programme'
  | 'job_posting'
  | 'news'
  | 'wealth_first';

/**
 * Kept deliberately separate from Evidence. A source that told us a firm exists
 * is not thereby allowed to tell us what the firm is.
 */
export interface Discovery {
  channel: DiscoveryChannel;
  sourceUrl: string;
  discoveredAt: string;
  /** CIK, EIN, company number - whatever the channel keys on. */
  externalId?: string;
  rawName: string;
}

export interface Signal {
  kind: 'investment' | 'fund_commitment' | 'key_hire' | 'news' | 'filing';
  summary: string;
  /** Undated signals are not intelligence. Records without a date are dropped at emit. */
  occurredAt: string;
  evidence: Evidence;
}

export interface Principal {
  fullName: Cell<string>;
  title: Cell<string>;
  /** Set when a statutory register records this person as controlling the entity. */
  controlBasis?: Cell<string>;
  linkedinUrl: Cell<string>;
  email: Cell<string>;
  phone: Cell<string>;
  location: Cell<string>;
}

export interface FamilyOffice {
  id: string;
  legalName: string;
  /** Every channel that independently surfaced this firm. Length > 1 is corroboration. */
  discoveries: Discovery[];
  classification: Classification;

  description: Cell<string>;
  investmentThesis: Cell<string>;
  sectors: Cell<string[]>;
  aum: Cell<number>;
  website: Cell<string>;
  linkedinUrl: Cell<string>;
  street: Cell<string>;
  postcode: Cell<string>;
  city: Cell<string>;
  region: Cell<string>;
  country: Cell<string>;

  principals: Principal[];
  signals: Signal[];

  createdAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
}

import { db, shortlist, type ShortlistQuery } from '@fo/db';

/**
 * The agent's tools (spec §8).
 *
 * Every tool returns `{ data, scope, excluded, limits }`. **Scope is mandatory.**
 * It is what lets the agent state in its answer what was searched and what was
 * left out — which Correction 8 requires of every user-visible sentence, and
 * which Stage 1 failed at when it silently answered a narrower question than the
 * one asked.
 *
 * Every tool reads **released claims only**. Candidate, held, quarantined and
 * withheld data is not reachable from here. That is not a filter the agent
 * applies and could forget; it is the only data these queries select.
 */

export interface ToolResult<T> {
  data: T;
  /** what was searched and what matched */
  scope: Record<string, unknown>;
  /** what was deliberately left out, and why */
  excluded: Array<{ reason: string; count: number }>;
  /** what this tool cannot tell you, stated rather than implied */
  limits: string[];
}

      required: ['entityId'],

import type {
  Claim,
  CommercialDecision,
  Entity,
  GateName,
  GateResult,
  ReleaseDecision,
} from '@fo/core/contract/index.js';

/**
 * The single path to released state.
 *
 * There is one function here and no setter for `status` is exported anywhere
 * else in the codebase. A claim that is released was released by this call, so
 * "how did this reach the customer?" always has exactly one answer.
 */
/**
 * Bumped when the standard changes. The `contract` job re-judges every claim
 * that has no decision at the current version, so a bump makes the scheduled
 * runs re-evaluate the whole file unattended.
 *
 * 2025-07-31.2 — the identity gate verifies a profile against every named
 * principal of the firm, not just the first one found. It had been comparing
 * /in/-varunmalhotra against a colleague called Elliott and quarantining 32
 * correct profiles.
 *
 * 2025-07-31.1 — attribution no longer strips a value that is entirely
 * stopwords. Oregon's state code "OR" was being filtered as the English
 * conjunction, leaving nothing to compare, and a correct claim was quarantined.
 * Previously quarantined claims are re-admitted by re-evaluation, not by an
 * UPDATE: the decision row records that it changed and why.
 */
export const POLICY_VERSION = '2025-07-31.2';

export function releaseDecision(
  claim: Claim,
  results: GateResult[],
  policyVersion = POLICY_VERSION,
): ReleaseDecision {
  const passed = results.filter((r) => r.outcome === 'passed').map((r) => r.gate);
  const failed = results.filter((r) => r.outcome === 'failed' || r.outcome === 'error').map((r) => r.gate);
  const skipped = results.filter((r) => r.outcome === 'skipped').map((r) => r.gate);

  const base = { claimId: claim.id, gatesPassed: passed, gatesFailed: failed, gatesSkipped: skipped, policyVersion };

  if (failed.length) {
    return { ...base, decision: 'quarantined' as const, reason: `failed: ${failed.join(', ')}` };
  }

  /**
   * PTC-2, and the reason `held` exists as a third outcome.
   *
   * A skipped gate is not a passed gate. Attribution can legitimately skip when

const FAMILY_WEALTH_VEHICLE =
  /\bfamily\s+(offices?|investments?|holdings?|capital|wealth|partners|trust|trustees|assets|ventures|advisors?|advisers?|office\s+services|management|legacy|financial)\b/i;

export function isFamilyWealthVehicleName(name: string): boolean {
  return FAMILY_WEALTH_VEHICLE.test(name);
}

export function assessEntity(
  entity: Entity,
  released: Claim[],
  policyVersion = POLICY_VERSION,
): CommercialDecision {
  const has = (f: string) => released.some((c) => c.field === f || c.field.endsWith('.' + f));
  // `fullName` moves from optional to required. The brief's floor is a contact
  // route that reaches a NAMED individual, so a record with no named person
  // cannot satisfy it however many other fields it carries -- and ADV and IAPD
  // publish firm identity with no individuals at all, which would have imported
  // exactly that.
  const required = ['legalName', 'country', 'fullName'];
  const commercial = ['website', 'city'];

  const missing = [...required.filter((f) => !has(f)), ...commercial.filter((f) => !has(f))];
  const meetsFloor = required.every(has) && commercial.filter(has).length >= 1;

  // A record must carry SOME affirmative sign that the firm is a family office.
  // Completeness is not evidence: without this, any company with an address and
  // a director qualified as long as its name contained "family" or "heritage"
  // somewhere. The strongest tier is a derived `entityClassification`; the
  // weakest is the firm's own registered name naming a family wealth vehicle.
  // Records resting only on the latter are counted and are visibly unclassified
  // in the export -- the standard is stated, not hidden.
  const classified = released.some((c) => c.field === 'entityClassification');
  if (!classified && !isFamilyWealthVehicleName(entity.canonicalName)) {
    return {
      entityId: entity.id,
      commercialState: 'withheld',
      reason:
        'no affirmative family-office evidence: neither a derived classification nor a ' +
        'registered name identifying a family wealth vehicle',
      missing,
      policyVersion,
    };
  }

  // An excluded institution fails regardless of how complete its record is.
  // Completeness is not the question here -- an insurance company with every
  // field filled is still not a family office.
  const excluded = excludedInstitution(entity.canonicalName);
  if (excluded) {
    return {
      entityId: entity.id,
      commercialState: 'withheld',
      reason: `excluded institution class: the name identifies a "${excluded}", which is not a family office`,
      missing,
      policyVersion,
    };
  }

  return {
    entityId: entity.id,
    commercialState: meetsFloor ? 'qualifying' : 'withheld',
    reason: meetsFloor
      ? 'holds identity claims and enough context to act on'
      : `below the commercial floor; missing ${missing.join(', ')}`,
    missing,
    policyVersion,
  };
}

I've read the product end to end — docs, pipeline, contract, agent, web app — and run the test suite. Here's the complete picture.

## What fo-intel (product name: **Sightline**) is

A two-deployable system built for the PolarityIQ Stage 2 "Differentiator" brief. The thesis is not "we have family office data" — it's **"every value carries the evidence that established it, and we'll show you what we refused to tell you and why."**

```
pipeline (GitHub Actions, scheduled)  ──writes──►  Neon Postgres  ◄──reads──  web (Vercel)
```
They share nothing but the database. The pipeline writes; the app reads **released claims only** and has no write path to claim state.

**Surfaces:** `/` Search (Stage 1 corpus, 50 records) · `/shortlist` retrieval extension (581 records) · `/agent` bounded agent · `/operations` what ran and what it refused.

## The architecture, and why it's shaped this way

Everything descends from one Stage 1 defect: of 155 delivered values carrying a verbatim quote, **93 cited a quote that didn't establish the value** — `build-dataset.ts:144` copied the firm's *classification* evidence onto nine unrelated fields at assembly time. The value was right; the binding was invented afterwards.

The fix isn't a better validator, it's a data model where that's **unexpressible**, defended three independent ways:
1. `Evidence` carries an unexported unique-symbol brand ([types.ts](packages/core/src/contract/types.ts)) — no module outside `contract/` can construct one.
2. `openExtractionEvent().assert()` is the only thing that mints role `establishing`, and it mints claim+evidence together ([extraction.ts](packages/core/src/contract/extraction.ts)). `attach()` cannot even *express* `establishing` in its type.
3. The database refuses it anyway — composite FK on a generated column (PTC-10), verified adversarially 6/6 by [verify-ptc10.ts](packages/db/src/verify-ptc10.ts).

**Claim lifecycle:** `candidate → validated → released → stale → superseded`, with `quarantined` off to the side. Six gates run in two bands (A: schema, attribution, value_type, contact_ownership, coherence; B: identity, conflict, freshness, commercial, copy). `skipped` is never collapsed into `passed` — that's PTC-2, and it's why `held` exists as a third release outcome. Release happens through exactly one function, [release/gate.ts](packages/pipeline/src/release/gate.ts), with a versioned `POLICY_VERSION` so tightening the standard demotes already-released claims on the next run.

**Trust is claim-level; commercial sufficiency is entity-level.** `assessEntity` decides `qualifying | withheld | unassessed` separately, and requires affirmative family-office evidence (derived classification, or a registered name naming a family wealth vehicle) plus an excluded-institution check — added after an audit found a bakery, a funeral home, a golf club and eleven hedge funds had qualified on an address and a director.

**Agentic boundary:** the model decides only *plan* and *compose*. Firm names are non-generative (`[[entityId]]` → server substitutes), every number is non-generative (`[[count:tool.field]]` → server substitutes), and seven deterministic output guards in [claims-guard.ts](packages/rag/src/agent/claims-guard.ts) can replace the whole answer. Extraction/validation/release contain no model-driven control flow at all.

**Honest state:** 740 entities · 581 qualifying · 54 strict-reachable against a requirement of 200 · 301 records with no classification · no AUM/mandate/sector data anywhere. The docs state this plainly rather than relabelling a weaker metric, and `ACCEPTANCE_M3.md` preserves a section that later proved wrong with the correction appended.

A disclosed filter that doesn't run is the exact inversion of the rule the file states two comments earlier.
- **E10 has a concrete root cause you didn't have.** In [run.ts](packages/rag/src/agent/run.ts), `evidenceChecks` are pushed with only `{entityId, field, completed, collectedAt}` — `passed`/`skipped`/`failed` are **never populated**, and `withheldByEntity` (line 222) is declared and never written to. So in `auditClaims`, `skipped` is always 0, which means the entire "skipped gate reported as a check that cleared the record" guard **cannot fire in production**, and `refused` is always 0, which means `unsupportedRefusal` fires on *any* refusal sentence even when a gate genuinely failed. The 127 tests pass because they inject the counts directly. ARCHITECTURE_NOTES §3 credits both as live guards.

One more not in your review: [search.tsx:894](apps/web/app/search.tsx:894) renders *"Reachable at the registered address above"* whenever phone and email are both absent — regardless of whether an address rendered. /**
 * Database access, shared by the pipeline (writes) and the web app (reads).
 *
 * Uses Neon's HTTP driver rather than a TCP pool because the web app runs as
 * serverless functions, where a connection pool has nowhere to live between
 * invocations.
 */
import { neon } from '@neondatabase/serverless';
import type { FamilyOffice } from '@fo/core';

export type Sql = ReturnType<typeof neon>;

let client: Sql | null = null;

export function db(): Sql {
  if (!client) {
    const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
    if (!url) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL not set');
    client = neon(url);
  }
  return client;
}

export interface FirmRow {
  id: string;
  legal_name: string;
  firm_type: string;
  type_confidence: number;
  country: string | null;
  city: string | null;
  region: string | null;
  has_phone: boolean;
  has_email: boolean;
  has_principal: boolean;
  signal_count: number;
  latest_signal_on: string | null;
  channel_count: number;
  record: FamilyOffice;
}

export interface RetrievedChunk {
  id: string;
  firm_id: string;
  kind: string;
  field_path: string;
  content: string;
  distance: number;
  legal_name: string;
  firm_type: string;
}

/**
 * Hybrid retrieval: structured predicates narrow the candidate set, semantic
 * similarity ranks within it.
 *
 * The order matters for correctness, not just speed. "Single-family offices in
 * Texas" is a filter, not a similarity question - embeddings will happily return
 * a Californian multi-family office that reads similarly, and the user has no way
 * to tell it violated their constraint.
 */

132:    FROM firms f

Replicated from source. Here's the mechanism, then my honest view — which is that your instinct is right that something is wrong here, but the reason you've given is the weakest one available, and acting on it would remove the wrong thing.

## Replication

The path is exact and matches what you saw:

- [answer.ts:280](packages/rag/src/answer.ts:280) — `checkAttribution(claims, …)` returns `{kept, dropped}`.
- [answer.ts:362](packages/rag/src/answer.ts:362) — `droppedClaims: dropped` ships the **full text plus reason** to the client.
- [search.tsx:924](apps/web/app/search.tsx:924) — the UI renders `droppedClaims.length` only, as *"2 draft statements did not survive verification…"*.

So the asymmetry is real and reproducible: full rejected text on the wire, count-only in the DOM. Your two drops are the two branches of [attribution.ts](packages/rag/src/attribution.ts) — Kopp failed `lexicalSupport` on a hard token (`55437`, line 150), Duquesne failed the `citedChunkIds.length === 0` guard (line 140) before any model saw it.

## The load argument does not hold

Measured against your own payload:

| | bytes | share |
|---|---|---|
| `droppedClaims` (both) | **374** | ~1.7% |
| `claims` (43 kept) | ~7,200 | ~33% |
| `firms` (11 records + `basis` blobs) | ~13,000 | ~60% |

And your timings say where the cost actually is: `auditMs` 4,804 of `totalMs` 8,323 — **58% of the response is the entailment call**, on a different provider, per request. Retrieval was 210 ms. Removing 374 bytes from a 22 KB response that took 8.3 seconds is not a performance fix; it's rounding error. If load is the goal, the levers are `MAX_SOURCES_IN_PROMPT`, the 11 full `basis` blobs, and caching the audit — not the drop list.

## "It shouldn't appear silently" — there's a stronger version of your argument than the one you made

The version that has teeth isn't payload, it's this: **the dropped text contains unverified assertions about real, named entities, and you're serving them to an anonymous client.** `"The registered address of Kopp Family Office, LLC is 701 CARLSON PARKWAY, SUITE 1030, BLOOMINGTON, MN, 55437"` is a sentence the system's own control judged unsupported, about a real firm at a real address, shipped over the wire anyway. That connects to **X3** (privacy and data-use sign-off), not to performance.

The counter-argument, which I think is stronger still: `droppedClaims` is the **receipt that the control fired**. This product's entire differentiator is *"here is what we refused to tell you and why."* The UI already tells the user two statements were removed — but not what or why, which is the part that would actually earn trust. Deleting the detail to save 374 bytes trades the thesis for nothing measurable. If anything the defensible direction is the opposite: surface it behind a disclosure on the page, so the DOM and the wire agree.

Either way, note what removal would *not* fix: the reason the claims were dropped.

## What I think is actually in this payload

You asked for my thoughts, so — reading your evidence rather than hunting for my own:

**The two drops are diagnostics pointing at a lane the auditor never reaches.** `checkAttribution` runs over `claims` only. `firms` is built *afterwards*, at [answer.ts:297](packages/rag/src/answer.ts:297), from `getFirms(citedFirmIds)`, and is never audited. Two lanes render on one page from one request; one is checked, one isn't. Your payload shows both lanes disagreeing, twice:

1. **Kopp.** The prose sentence was killed for the postcode `55437`. The card that shipped carries `address: "701 CARLSON PARKWAY, SUITE 1030, BLOOMINGTON, 55305"` — while its own `basis.address` quotes *"8400 NORMANDALE LAKE BOULEVARD SUITE 1450 BLOOMINGTON, MN 55437"*. Different street, different postcode, presented as the evidence for the value above it. That is the Kopp assembly defect the Stage 2 spec names as gate 6's own example, still rendering.

2. **Duquesne.** *"A direct phone number is on record for Duquesne Family Office"* was dropped as uncited — and the card ships `phone: "212-830-6500"` regardless. On a question that explicitly asked for the phone number.

The structural reason, which I'd want you to confirm independently: **the Search tab reads the Stage 1 tables** — [index.ts:80](packages/db/src/index.ts:80) queries `firms` / `firm_chunks`, not `s2_*`. Those records carry the Stage 1 `Cell<T>.evidence` array, the shape [core/src/index.ts](packages/core/src/index.ts) explicitly refuses to re-export because it is *"the loose, assignable shape that made the mis-wiring possible."* None of the Stage 2 guarantees — extraction-event binding, PTC-10, the composite FK — apply to anything on that page. But it renders a "How this was confirmed" panel that is visually indistinguishable in kind from the Stage 2 evidence surfaces.

Against your exclusion list: **S1** says Search covers 50 records rather than 581 — a coverage complaint. It does not say the 50 are un-re-derived Stage 1 records whose value↔evidence binding is the exact defect Stage 2 was built to make unexpressible, still shipping evidence panels. **L1** is the Shortlist tier badge, different surface and different mechanism. So this is adjacent to the review but not a repeat, as far as I can tell.

## My recommendation

Don't file this as a payload/performance issue — it won't survive scrutiny, and the fix would delete the audit trail while leaving both contradictions in place. If you want a finding from this session, the durable one is the two-lane gap, and your dropped claims are the cleanest possible evidence for it: **the system caught the bad address in the sentence and shipped it in the card.**

# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis

A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Creating with docx-js — gotchas

`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.

## Verify the output

After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
```

`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).

## Editing existing documents

Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.

```bash
unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)
python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
```

Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).

**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author "<the name you redlined under>"` (needs `--original`) — it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.

To produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.

Accepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way — they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:

- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.
- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.

An empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.

## Comments

Comments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper — directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:

```bash
# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Fees & expenses cap is too low"
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Agreed" --parent 0

# Against a .docx directly
python scripts/comment.py contract.docx "This cap is too low" -o annotated.docx
```

The script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text — until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.

## Dependencies

`docx` (npm, preinstalled — install only if `require('docx')` fails) · `pandoc` · LibreOffice (`soffice`) · `pdftoppm` (Poppler)

`canonical` holds exactly one key — Duquesne. `canonical.has("Kopp Family Office")` is false, so Kopp's request is bound to `[...canonical.keys()][0]`, which is **Duquesne's id**.

Later, someone cleaned them up in bulk: six of them were closed at once, in two batches of three, and each batch got stamped with the exact same end time down to the millisecond.

The problem is what that did to the numbers. Every run that actually finished normally in your system takes under 41 minutes — that's true across all 118. But those six cleaned-up rows now show durations of 44 hours, 50 hours, and 74 hours, because their "end time" is really just the moment somebody ran the cleanup, not the moment they stopped. One of them is a `contract` job, which your own acceptance report says does almost nothing when the policy version hasn't changed. The log says it ran for three days.

Nothing in the file flags these as reconstructed. Six of the seven closed-out rows have no reason recorded at all — just an empty failures list.

**The part that makes it checkable.** Your Architecture Notes, section 4, says this out loud:

> "Two such rows are in the exported log, not hidden."

Meaning: two of these unfinished rows are still sitting in the export where a reviewer can see them. But there are zero. They were all closed. So the document and the file it points to flatly disagree, and it's the document making the positive claim. Anyone can check it in one command.

**Why I think it matters.** Your whole system is built on the idea that "we didn't check this" and "we checked this and it was fine" must never look the same. That's PTC-7, it's in your spec, it's the thing the product sells. Here, "the process died and we never learned when it stopped" got overwritten with a specific timestamp that reads like a real measurement. And your acceptance report had already spotted the original problem — it says a stuck row makes the window queries ambiguous — so the fix traded an ambiguous row for a false one, without saying so anywhere.

**It's not already known.** I searched the 72-item false-statement register and the QA report for anything about run logs, aborted runs, durations, or stuck rows. Nothing. The register's section on Stage 2 build artifacts is all about the goal traces, commit messages and stale counts — nobody has looked at this file.

**What I'm not claiming.** All six cleaned-up rows were manual runs, not scheduled ones. So this does not touch your evidence for unattended operation — the 44 scheduled runs and the 94.8-hour window are intact, and I checked the staleness events separately and they hold up too. This is about the log being accurate, not about faking the operating window. You should say that yourself, up front, because it's the first thing a reviewer will test and it makes everything else you say more credible.

import { readFileSync, readdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { connect, withRetry } from './connect.js';

const sql = connect();

// fileURLToPath, not .pathname: the repo lives under a directory with a space
// in its name and .pathname leaves it percent-encoded.
const dir = fileURLToPath(new URL('./migrations/', import.meta.url));
const files = readdirSync(dir).filter((f) => f.endsWith('.sql')).sort();

/**
 * Split on semicolons that actually terminate a statement.
 *
 * A plain .split(';') shreds any DO $$ ... $$ block into fragments that each
 * fail on their own -- and 003 needs one, because ALTER TABLE ADD CONSTRAINT has
 * no IF NOT EXISTS and migrations re-run. So track dollar-quoted bodies and
 * ordinary string literals, and only break outside both.
 */
function splitStatements(sqlText: string): string[] {
  const out: string[] = [];
  let buf = '';
  let i = 0;
  let tag: string | null = null; // open dollar-quote tag, e.g. "$$" or "$fn$"
  let inString = false;

  while (i < sqlText.length) {
    const ch = sqlText[i];

    if (tag) {
      if (sqlText.startsWith(tag, i)) {
        buf += tag;
        i += tag.length;
        tag = null;
        continue;
      }
    } else if (inString) {
      if (ch === "'") inString = false;
    } else if (ch === "'") {
      inString = true;
    } else if (ch === '$') {
      const m = /^\$[A-Za-z_]*\$/.exec(sqlText.slice(i));
      if (m) {
        tag = m[0];
        buf += tag;
        i += tag.length;
        continue;
      }
    } else if (ch === ';') {
      if (buf.trim()) out.push(buf.trim());
      buf = '';
      i++;
      continue;
    }

    buf += ch;
    i++;
  }
  if (buf.trim()) out.push(buf.trim());
  return out;
}

for (const file of files) {
  const ddl = readFileSync(dir + file, 'utf8');
  // strip comment lines before splitting: splitting first and discarding
  // anything starting with "--" silently drops every statement with a comment
  // above it, which is most of them. (Learned this the hard way in Stage 1.)
  const body = ddl
    .split('\n')
    .filter((l) => !l.trim().startsWith('--'))
    .join('\n');
  const statements = splitStatements(body);

  console.log(`\n${file}  (${statements.length} statements)`);
  let failed = 0;
  for (const stmt of statements) {
    const label = stmt.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').slice(0, 66);
    // A transient fault on statement 1 cascades into every dependent statement,
    // so a DNS blip would otherwise read as a schema error.
    try {
      await withRetry(() => sql.query(stmt), 4, label);
      console.log(`  ok    ${label}`);
    } catch (err) {
      failed++;
      console.log(`  FAIL  ${label}\n        ${err instanceof Error ? err.message : err}`);
    }
  }
  if (failed) console.log(`  ${failed} statement(s) failed`);
}

const [c] = (await sql`
  SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS n FROM information_schema.tables
  WHERE table_schema='public' AND table_name LIKE 's2_%'
`) as unknown as Array<{ n: number }>;
console.log(`\ns2_* tables present: ${c?.n ?? 0}`);
=== 003 head ===
-- M3 · The operating record.
--
-- The brief asks for complete run logs across a 48-hour unattended window, and
-- for evidence that the system handled a real dependency failure and a real
-- staleness event. Those are claims about behaviour, so they need rows that were
-- written while the behaviour happened -- not a narrative composed afterwards.

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------- runs

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS s2_run (
  id                 TEXT PRIMARY KEY,

  -- `schedule` is the one that counts toward the operating window. A run that
  -- was triggered by hand cannot evidence unattended operation, so the trigger
  -- is recorded rather than assumed.

## What it does and why

**Adds two columns: `closed_at` and `close_reason`.**
There was nowhere to put either. That's the root of it — the schema gave the cleanup no way to say "this row was closed by hand at this time, for this reason," so the only field available was `ended_at`, which means something else entirely. One says when the run stopped; the other says when we stopped waiting for it. Having both means the row never has to lie about which it is.

**Makes the four counters nullable.**
This is the one you'll want to check. They were `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, which made two completely different situations look identical: a `contract` run that legitimately evaluated nothing, and a run killed before it could write what it did. About forty of the first kind sit in the export next to seven of the second, all reading `0`. No validation rule can separate them while the column can't hold NULL — that's why my second draft of the rules was unsound. So this isn't tidying; it's the change that makes "we never found out" expressible at all.

**Adds three constraints, marked `NOT VALID`.**
Database-level, matching how PTC-10 works — a rule the database enforces rather than one the writer is trusted to follow:

- an end time and a closure time can never both be set
- a closure time must have a reason
- a terminal run must record when it terminated, one way or the other

`NOT VALID` means Postgres enforces these on **every future write** but does not check the existing rows. That's deliberate: the seven historical rows violate all three, and they're submitted evidence. Validating them would force rewriting the record this fix exists to describe. Keep the wrong thing visible, stop it happening again.

## What I checked

The migration runner strips comments then splits on semicolons, and my `DO $$` blocks contain semicolons inside them — a bad split would fail silently. I ran the project's own splitter against the file: **14 statements, all `$$` blocks balanced**, the DO blocks intact. Every statement is re-runnable (`IF NOT EXISTS`, and `DROP NOT NULL`/`DROP DEFAULT` are no-ops when already applied).

Nothing breaks today, because no NULLs exist yet. But once steps 2 and 3 start writing them:

- `stage2-reads.ts:16-17` types the counters as `number` — needs `number | null`
- `operations/page.tsx:74-76` renders them straight into the table — a NULL would show as an empty cell, which is the same "unknown looks like a value" problem in the UI
- `export-operating-window.ts` doesn't emit the two new columns yet

I'll handle all three in Step 5 rather than leaving them to surface later.

import 'dotenv/config';
import { neon } from '@neondatabase/serverless';
import { installResilientDns } from '@fo/core/net/dns.js';

/**
 * The only way Stage 2 code opens a database connection.
 *
 * Neon's serverless driver talks HTTP, so it goes through undici and inherits
 * undici's defaults: the system resolver, and a 10-second connect timeout. On
 * this machine the router's resolver returns intermittent SERVFAILs, which is
 * the whole reason `installResilientDns` exists -- it swaps in public resolvers
 * and raises the connect timeout to 15s.
 *
 * Stage 1 installed it as an import side-effect in three pipeline modules. The
 * Stage 2 database scripts were written without it and failed with
 * ConnectTimeoutError against api.*.neon.tech, which reads like Neon being down
 * and is actually local DNS. Routing every connection through one function is
 * what stops the next script from forgetting.
 */
export function connect(url = process.env.DATABASE_URL) {
  if (!url) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL not set');
  installResilientDns();
  return neon(url);
}

## What changed

**Non-empty reason required.** `close_reason IS NOT NULL` alone would have accepted `''`. There's also a subtler trap I hit while writing it: a CHECK constraint **passes when its expression evaluates to NULL**, so `length(btrim(close_reason)) > 0` on its own would have let a NULL reason straight through — `btrim(NULL)` → NULL → `NULL > 0` → NULL → passes. The constraint now spells out both parts, and `btrim` rejects whitespace-only too.

**A close reason now belongs only to an aborted run.** The `running` and normally-finished branches require `close_reason IS NULL`. Otherwise a completed run could carry one and read as though its row had been closed for it when it ended on its own.

**The TypeScript rules now match the database exactly.** That cost one piece of leniency I'd built in: `orphan_closed_without_reason` used to accept a `failures` entry in place of a reason, which spared the 10-minute-timeout row. The database names `close_reason` specifically, so I dropped the exemption. **That row is now flagged too — it's seven, not six.** It does carry its message, but in `failures_json`, which records what went wrong *while running*, not why the row was closed *afterwards*. Different fact, different field. The test now asserts both halves so the distinction is on the record rather than buried.

New rule `close_reason_without_administrative_close` mirrors the other half. 21 lifecycle tests now, up from 19.

Step 2 done. **157/157, typecheck clean.** Production untouched; scratch cluster stopped.

## What I built

Two files plus tests:

- [close-orphaned-runs.ts](packages/pipeline/src/run/close-orphaned-runs.ts) — the logic, split into a pure `selectOrphans()` (testable with no database) and the write.
- [jobs/close-orphaned-runs.ts](packages/pipeline/src/jobs/close-orphaned-runs.ts) — the runnable entry, following the `jobs/` pattern rather than the Stage 1 `cli.ts`.

**It never writes `ended_at`.** It writes `closed_at` — when the row was closed, which is a fact — and a `close_reason`. It doesn't touch the counters, so after the migration a killed run reports NULL rather than 0.

**The reason says only what was observed: silence.** Not "killed", not "timed out", not "crashed" — none of that is visible from a database row. There's a test asserting the reason contains no cause-of-death words, because guessing there would be the same error as an end time nobody measured, just in a different field.

**The threshold is measured, not picked.** A run counts as dead after **30 minutes of silence**, judged on its last log line rather than total duration — a long run that's still logging is alive, a short one that stopped isn't. Across the 108 healthy completed runs in the export, the worst gap between consecutive log lines is 17.3 minutes and the 95th percentile is 4 minutes. 30 gives ~1.7× headroom, and there's a test pinning that a 17-minute pause is never swept.

**Dry run by default.** It prints what it would close and writes nothing; `CLOSE_ORPHANS_APPLY=1` commits. This operates on the operating record itself, so the version that changes history should be the one you have to ask for.

**It excludes itself.** A sweeper that ran long enough would eventually pass its own threshold and close its own row — the kind of bug that only shows up in production. There's a test for it.

## What I verified beyond the unit tests

The tests only exercise the pure selector, so I ran the function's **actual SQL** against the scratch database with two seeded rows — one dead (silent 90 minutes), one alive (logged a minute ago):

- the dead run closed to `status=aborted, ended_at=NULL, closed_at=set, counters=NULL`
- **the live run was untouched**, still `running`
- re-running the same `UPDATE` affected **0 rows** and left the original reason intact — the `AND status='running'` clause makes it idempotent
- a blank reason is still refused by the constraint

Two tests tie the pieces together: the row this function produces is fed into the Step 0 checker and must come back **clean**, and the historical hand-swept shape is asserted to still fail. If the writer ever produced a row its own audit rejected, that would break.

### Assistant · 2026-08-15T12:43:06.615Z

Step 2 corrected. **162/162, typecheck clean.** Scratch cluster stopped; production untouched.

## The three safety fixes

**Dry run is now the default in the function itself.** `dryRun ?? true`. Importing `closeOrphanedRuns` and calling it bare reports what it would do and writes nothing — the destructive behaviour has to be asked for by name. There's a behavioural test for this, not a source-text check: both I/O seams are injectable, so the test runs with no database, hands it a store that **throws on any write**, and calls it bare. If the default ever flips, that test fails loudly instead of the change reaching an operating database.

**The closure is atomic.** The status check and the silence recheck are now in the same `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` clause, with `RETURNING id`. A run that logged while we were deciding fails the condition instead of being closed on a stale read.

**The ordering is reversed, and that mattered more than I realised.** The first draft wrote the closure log line *before* the update — so a run that came back to life would have received a `run_closed_administratively` entry describing a closure that never happened. **A false statement in the operating log, written by the fix for false statements in the operating log.** Now the update decides: only a row it actually changed gets logged, and only such a row is reported.

I also split the result into `selected` (met the threshold) and `closed` (an `UPDATE` actually changed it). Reporting an intention as an outcome is the same category of error this whole branch is about, so they're now different fields and the job prints them differently.

## Verified in real SQL, not just the fake

Two rows on the scratch database, both silent at selection time, then one logs again before the update:

```
run_dead     -> RETURNING gave 1 row(s)
run_revived  -> RETURNING gave 0 row(s)

run_dead:    status=aborted | ended_at=NULL | closed_at set=true  | counters=NULL
run_revived: status=running | ended_at=NULL | closed_at set=false | counters=NULL
```

The revived run is completely untouched — still `running`, no closure time, and no closure log line written for it. That's your race, proved against Postgres rather than a mock.

Four new race tests cover it at the unit level too, including that a revived run doesn't block the genuinely dead ones from closing.

## One thing worth flagging

I need to be honest about the guarantee: the recheck is *one statement*, which is a very large improvement over a stale read, but under `READ COMMITTED` a concurrent log insert committing at exactly the wrong moment is still theoretically possible. The consequence would be closing a run that had just revived — recoverable, since the row keeps its reason and nothing is deleted. I've said this in the code comment rather than claiming atomicity I can't fully back.

Also, typecheck caught a real break I introduced while making `connect()` lazy — `sql` fell out of scope for the default store. Fixed, and the connection now opens only on the writing path, so dry runs and every test need no database at all.

Ready for **Step 3 — counters written as work commits**.

Step 3 done. **171/171, typecheck clean.** First modification to an existing file: `runner.ts`.

## What I implemented

**The counters are now written as work commits, not once at the end.**

The old behaviour was a single write inside `finish()`, in the same statement as the end time. A `SIGKILL` never reaches it, so the row kept the schema default of `0` — and after the hand-written cleanup gave that row a status and an end time, it read as a run that completed and did nothing. `run_20260730191237_40bd4888` is the case: 43 log lines, 42 decisions including a quarantine, and `claimsQuarantined: 0` on the row above them.

The log lines survived that kill because they're written as they occur. So the counters now work the same way.

**Three places they get persisted, and no job had to change** — jobs already mutate the shared `counts` object, so I hooked the flush rather than the call sites:

- **On every log line**, throttled to at most once every 5 seconds. Jobs log as they work, so that's the natural heartbeat and nobody has to remember to call anything.
- **On every checkpoint, unthrottled.** A checkpoint means "this unit's writes are committed" — exactly the moment the row should agree with the checkpoint. If the process dies immediately after, the two tell the same story.
- **On `finish()`**, unchanged.

I also exposed `run.flushCounts()` so a job can force it at a boundary of its own.

**Two deliberate properties.** The flush writes *only* the four counters — never `ended_at` or `status`, since a `running` row carrying an end time would violate the new constraint as well as being false. And it **never throws**: losing a counter write is a degraded record, but failing a whole job because a counter write failed would be worse than the problem it guards. It logs `count_flush_failed` to stdout and continues, same as a failed log write.

**The throttle is a policy module, not a line in the runner** — [count-flush.ts](packages/pipeline/src/run/count-flush.ts), pure and tested, because `runner.ts` can't be imported without a database connection. Unchanged counters are never written even when forced, so an idle `contract` run still costs zero extra statements.

## The end-to-end proof

On scratch, the full lifecycle of a killed run:

```
at start       -> touched=NULL  quarantined=NULL          (nothing counted yet)
after flush    -> touched=41    quarantined=1   running   ended_at=NULL
after closure  -> touched=41    quarantined=1   aborted   ended_at=NULL  closed_at=set
```

That's the row the historical defect got wrong, now telling the truth: 41 records touched, 1 claim quarantined, no end time claimed, and a stated reason. Compare with what's in the submitted export for the same shape — `0 / 0 / aborted / ended_at 74 hours later`.

9 new policy tests, including one that reconstructs that exact production row.

## One thing I found but did not fix

`finish()` writes `run_finished` to **stdout only** — it never reaches `s2_run_log`. That's why no run in the database has a completion record, including the 109 healthy ones, and it's why I couldn't anchor the lifecycle rules on "has a completion log line" back in Step 0.

Adding it would make the operating log complete and would let that rule become checkable. It's a two-line change, but it's outside what you scoped for this step, so I've left it. Say the word and I'll fold it into Step 4 or leave it alone.

### Assistant · 2026-08-15T14:30:51.745Z

Step 3 corrected. **173/173, typecheck clean.** Scratch cluster stopped; production untouched.

## 1. The opening zeros no longer destroy the unknown state

You were right, and it was worse than a cosmetic issue. `startRun` logs `run_started` before any work exists, and the log path carries the throttled flush. Seeded with `null`, that first line counted as a change — so **every run immediately wrote `0/0/0/0` over the NULLs the INSERT had left.** The row said "this run did nothing" from the moment it was born, and a kill before the first unit was indistinguishable from a run that genuinely did nothing. The migration created the unknown state and the flush erased it a millisecond later.

`newFlushState()` now seeds `lastFlushed` with the zero snapshot, so the opening zeros count as already-persisted. The first write happens when something actually moves. `lastFlushAt` stays 0, so that first real change is still written immediately.

## 2. The silent loops now persist

`contract` and `backfill-classification` both run through hundreds of records with no log line and no checkpoint, so nothing was persisting their counters — the fix didn't reach them. Both loops now call `run.flushCounts({ throttled: true })` per item.

Throttled, not forced: a forced write per record would be a statement per record. The test simulates 500 records at 40ms each and asserts both bounds — **no more than one write per interval**, and **a kill loses at most one interval's worth of counting** rather than the whole run. That's the actual guarantee; the tail is always lost, and the point is that it's bounded.

I extended `flushCounts` to take `{ throttled: true }` rather than adding a second method, so there's one way to persist counters with the boundary stated at the call site.

## 3. The checkpoint and the counter flush are now one statement

This was the sharpest of the three. The counter write swallowed its own errors, so the cursor could advance past work whose count was never recorded — and no later run would ever go back for it. The record would under-report permanently with nothing to indicate it.

Now the counter update is a CTE and the checkpoint upsert reads from it:

```sql
WITH counted AS (UPDATE s2_run SET ... WHERE id = ... RETURNING id)
INSERT INTO s2_checkpoint (...) SELECT ..., counted.id FROM counted
ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET ...
RETURNING id
```

If the run row is missing, the CTE returns nothing, the `INSERT ... SELECT` inserts nothing, and **the cursor does not move**. One statement, one transaction — they cannot disagree. If it returns no rows the method throws rather than letting a caller believe it advanced.

Proved on scratch both ways:

```
A. run exists    -> run: touched=41 quarantined=1   cursor: CURSOR-1 units=7
B. run missing   -> INSERT 0 0                      cursor: still CURSOR-1 units=7
```

A third case fell out by accident and is worth reporting: my first attempt hit a foreign-key error on the checkpoint insert, and **the counter update rolled back with it** — the run still showed `NULL`. That's the atomicity working under a real failure rather than a simulated one.

`run_finished` left unchanged, as you asked.

Ready for **Step 4 — wiring the lifecycle rules into the `contract` job**.

## Step 4 — the audit, wired

`contract` now audits every run row on every execution, the same way it already audits claims for PTC-1. Violations partition three ways:

- **legacy** — runs started before `LEGACY_BEFORE` (2026-08-15). All 7 historical rows land here. Counted and logged on **every** run, never fatal.
- **blocking** — anything written after the cutoff. Fails the job.
- **warnings** — the two completed-run counter gaps. Never fatal, always reported.

I used a **timestamp cutoff rather than a list of run ids** deliberately: an id list can be quietly extended to excuse a new row, whereas a cutoff can only ever excuse the past, and the past is finite. Tests assert `blocking` is empty against the submitted export, that an identical defect dated after the cutoff **does** block, and that a correctly-closed run after the cutoff does not.

The rules now accept aggregated decision counts, so the audit is one query rather than pulling ~1,500 decision rows.

The export writes to **`operating-window.corrected.json`**, never over the submitted file. That's the point: the two side by side are the proof, and regenerating in place would replace the artifact whose defects this branch describes.

The `note` no longer claims the file contains rows left `running` — it never did. It now describes what's actually there, including what a `null` counter means.

Both readers were about to reintroduce the confusion at the render: `stage2-reads.ts` typed the counters as `number`, and `operations/page.tsx` printed them straight into the table, so a NULL would have shown as an empty cell. The page now prints **"not recorded"** with a tooltip, and a new column distinguishes a run that reported its own end from one whose row was *closed* for it, reason on hover.

                counters: touched=25  created=50  quarantined=2
```

**Under the old code those counters would read `0/0/0`.** That is the exact defect from `run_20260730191237_40bd4888` — 42 decisions above a row claiming zero — not reproduced, but prevented.

## The full sequence

**1. Migration over real historical rows.** All 7 migrations applied to the branch. Counters became nullable, `closed_at`/`close_reason` appeared, the constraint landed `NOT VALID`, and **all 7 historical rows survived untouched, still carrying their `ended_at`**. A new bad write was refused immediately. That's the production-safety question answered on real data rather than a simulation.

**2. First kill — the log-triggered flush.** Killed at unit ~25, before any checkpoint. Counters `25/50/2` persisted purely by the throttled flush hanging off `log()`.

**3. Dry run is genuinely inert.** I re-inspected the row after the dry run: still `running`, nothing written. Then `CLOSE_ORPHANS_APPLY=1` produced:

```
status: aborted   ended_at: NULL   closed_at: 2026-08-15T15:10:54Z
counters: touched=25 created=50 quarantined=2   (intact)
```

**4. Second kill — the atomic checkpoint.** Moved the checkpoint to unit 8 so it would fire. Result:

```
checkpoint: HARNESS-UNIT-8  units=8
counters  : touched=8  created=16
log lines : 1
```

Only **one** log line, so those counters came *solely* from the checkpoint's write — the cursor and the counters agree exactly, because they moved in one statement.

**5. The audit, and the real `contract` job.**

```
runsAudited: 322   blocking: 0   legacy: 23 across 7 runs   warnings: 6
```

Job completed. The seven historical rows are reported on every execution and block nothing; the two new correctly-closed runs — both dated *after* the cutoff, so eligible to block — raise nothing at all.

**6. Defence in depth.** I tried inserting a post-cutoff row in the historical shape to prove the blocking path. It never reached the audit: **the database refused it**. The audit is the second line; the constraint is the first.

## One honest note on method

`contract` had zero claims to evaluate on the branch, and `readjudicate-postal` never touches `run.counts` — so no shipped job could exercise the counter path. I drove the **real `withRun`** with a synthetic job body instead. `startRun`, `log`, the counters, `checkpoint` and the flush policy are all production code imported unmodified; only the loop that increments them is a harness. That is the right target anyway, since both the defect and the fix live in `runner.ts` rather than in any one job — but the distinction belongs in the write-up rather than glossed over.

## State of things

- Local: **178/178, typecheck clean**, 16 files on `fix/orphaned-run-integrity`, **nothing committed**.
- The branch now holds 3 extra rows from testing: 2 correctly-closed harness runs and 1 completed `contract` run. Worth knowing before you delete it — and they're useful evidence if you want to inspect them yourself first.
- `.env.scratch.local` still exists and is gitignored. The connection string was never printed and is not in this transcript.
